anabaptist.church_discipline:
Anabaptists understand the church as a community of believers who have committed themselves to follow Christ and to hold one another accountable. Following the pattern Jesus gives in the Gospel of Matthew, a member who persists in serious sin is first spoken to privately, then with others, and finally, if there is no repentance, may be set outside the fellowship. This is called the ban.

The purpose is described as restoration, not punishment: to protect the purity of the church and to call the person back. Where it is practiced most strictly, as among the Amish, it includes shunning, meaning limits on ordinary social and business contact with the person until they repent. Many Mennonite groups practice discipline more gently or seldom formally, so the practice varies widely across the Anabaptist family.
anabaptist.infant_baptism:
Anabaptists practice believer's baptism: baptism is given only to those who are old enough to make a personal confession of faith and to commit themselves to follow Christ and to the community of the church. The name Anabaptist, meaning rebaptizer, came from the early practice of baptizing adults who had been baptized as infants.

They do not consider infant baptism to be baptism in the biblical sense, since an infant cannot repent or believe. Children are understood to be safe in God's care, and are taught the faith until they can make their own decision. Baptism is therefore both a sign of forgiveness and a public promise to live as a disciple and to be accountable to the congregation. This is why the timing of baptism matters deeply.
anabaptist.foot_washing:
Some Anabaptist groups practice foot washing as an ordinance, following Jesus' washing of the disciples' feet in the Gospel of John and his instruction that they should do likewise. It is understood as a sign of humility, service and love within the community, and it often accompanies the observance of communion.

Practice differs. It is regular among the Amish and many Old Order and conservative Mennonite groups, while many mainstream Mennonite churches do it only occasionally or not at all. Where it is practiced, believers usually wash and dry one another's feet in pairs, men with men and women with women. It is treated as a serious act of obedience and of reconciliation, and less as a symbol alone.
anabaptist.pacifism:
Anabaptists hold that Jesus' teaching to love enemies and not to return evil for evil applies to his followers in the world, and so they do not take part in war or in violence. Many use the word nonresistance, meaning that the Christian does not resist an evildoer by force but answers with love and patient suffering. Others prefer to speak of pacifism or peacemaking, and work actively for justice and reconciliation.

This conviction goes back to the early Anabaptists, some of whom suffered persecution because they refused to bear the sword. It has shaped a long tradition of conscientious objection and service work. Anabaptist groups differ in how far they engage with government and public life, but peace as a mark of discipleship is central to the whole family.
anabaptist.oaths:
Anabaptists do not swear oaths. They understand Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount, that his followers should not swear at all but let their yes be yes and their no be no, as a direct command. A Christian's word should be so reliable that no oath is needed.

In legal settings Anabaptists ask to make an affirmation in place of an oath, and many countries allow this. In some stricter groups, the objection also affects willingness to hold certain public offices or serve on juries where oaths are required. The conviction is less about a ritual formula than about truthfulness in every conversation, and about not suggesting that a person's ordinary speech needs any additional guarantee.
anabaptist.head_covering:
In some Anabaptist communities, women wear a prayer covering or head covering, a small cap or scarf, as a way of following the teaching about prayer and headship in the First Letter to the Corinthians. It is understood as a sign of order in creation and of a woman's prayerful place in the church, and it is worn by many Amish and by Old Order and conservative Mennonite women, often throughout the day.

Practice varies. Hutterite women commonly wear a head scarf, while most mainstream Mennonite congregations no longer require any covering. Where it is kept, the covering is regarded as a serious matter of obedience and of community identity, and the style of it often shows which group a woman belongs to. Anabaptists who do not wear one generally read the passage as reflecting the customs of its own time.
